title: Blockchains are fast enough. Are they ready for financial markets?
gist: a16z crypto argues throughput is no longer the bottleneck for onchain finance — aggregate blockchain throughput is up more than 100x in five years and some production systems clear tens of thousands of transactions per second — so the binding constraints are now predictable inclusion, explicit ordering rules, and pre-execution privacy. It frames the remaining gaps as resilience (Strong Chain Quality, multi-route blockspace access), ordering discretion and MEV that risk recreating TradFi's order-flow asymmetries, and encryption (timelock, threshold) to protect trading intent before execution.

themes.theme: Throughput commoditized as the new baseline

insights.claim: Aggregate blockchain throughput has grown more than 100x in five years, and some production systems can now process tens of thousands of transactions per second.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Raw TPS is no longer a differentiator when underwriting L1/L2 tokens — screen for execution guarantees instead of benchmark speed.
insights.quote: aggregate blockchain throughput has grown more than 100x in five years, and some production systems can now process tens of thousands of transactions per second
insights.locator: For years, capacity was an obvious bottleneck

insights.claim: Throughput is becoming less differentiated across many production blockchains, shifting the competitive frontier for financial use cases away from cost and transactions-per-second.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Expect the 'fastest chain' marketing narrative to lose pricing power; value should accrue to chains with credible inclusion, ordering, and privacy guarantees.
insights.quote: throughput is becoming less differentiated across many production systems
insights.locator: For years, debates around blockchain readiness

insights.claim: High throughput only makes onchain finance plausible; predictable inclusion and clear ordering rules are what make it usable when timing matters and under real market pressure.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Use a two-stage readiness test — capacity first, then predictability — when assessing which chains institutions can actually route flow through.
insights.quote: High throughput makes onchain finance plausible. Predictable inclusion and clear ordering rules make it usable when timing matters and under real market pressure.
insights.locator: High throughput makes onchain finance plausible

insights.claim: Bringing assets, ownership records, and execution rules into a shared system that no single counterparty controls does not by itself make a blockchain ready for the scale and constraints of global financial markets.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Discount pitches that treat decentralization alone as institutional-readiness; demand evidence of behavior under congestion, outages, and attacks.
insights.quote: This does not, however, make blockchains automatically ready for the scale and constraints they’d have to contend with in global financial markets.
insights.locator: Finance is one of the most obvious use cases

insights.claim: Predictability for onchain markets decomposes into exactly two guarantees: guarantees on inclusion (censorship resistance) and guarantees on ordering.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A clean two-axis checklist for diligencing any chain or sequencer pitching institutional trading.
insights.quote: predictability requires two kinds of guarantees: (1) guarantees on inclusion — or censorship resistance — and (2) guarantees on ordering
insights.locator: In other words, predictability requires two kinds

insights.claim: Payments and markets have fundamentally different latency tolerances: a second of uncertainty is acceptable for everyday payments, while in markets every millisecond can decide whether participants trust the venue at all.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Stablecoin-payment infrastructure and onchain-trading infrastructure are separate investable categories with different technical bars — do not price them off the same benchmarks.
insights.quote: For everyday payments, a second of uncertainty is probably fine, but for markets, every millisecond can decide whether participants trust the venue at all.
insights.locator: Transactions need to land on schedule

insights.claim: On an onchain order book, a cancel order that lands too late lets someone trade against a stale price, and market makers price that risk in by widening spreads, producing worse execution for every participant.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Spread width on onchain venues is a direct, observable proxy for the chain's timing reliability — monitor it as a readiness metric.
insights.quote: If a trader’s cancel order lands too late, someone can trade against a stale price. Market makers price in that risk by widening spreads, which means worse prices for everyone.
insights.locator: Take an onchain order book, for instance

insights.claim: Financial institutions executing trades onchain and issuing stablecoins and tokenized assets require reliable access, predictable transaction processing rules, and control over when sensitive information becomes visible — and those guarantees must hold through congestion, outages, and attacks.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Stress behavior, not steady-state benchmarks, is the gating factor for institutional tokenization volumes migrating onchain.
insights.quote: Those guarantees must also hold through congestion, outages, and attacks.
insights.locator: As financial institutions start executing trades onchain

insights.claim: Resilience — whether a participant can submit an order at all without depending on a single gatekeeper — is a distinct and earlier problem than sequencing, which only governs an order's position once it has already hit the chain.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Separate 'can I get in' from 'where do I land' when evaluating rollups and appchains; single-sequencer designs fail the first test regardless of ordering fairness.
insights.quote: Sequencing determines an order’s place relative to other orders, once it hits the chain, while resilience starts a step earlier.
insights.locator: Sequencing determines an order’s place relative

insights.claim: A single randomly staked node controlling transaction ingress into an exchange like NYSE every second would be able to exert extreme market power over traders on that exchange.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A sharp analogy for why single-sequencer chains are structurally unacceptable to institutional trading desks.
insights.quote: Imagine we selected a randomly staked node worldwide to control transaction ingress into NYSE every second.
insights.locator: Even with good ordering rules

insights.claim: Blockchain developers are shifting the target standard from eventual inclusion to instantaneous inclusion, so that a valid transaction reaching the network on time is included immediately rather than 'soon'.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Watch for chains marketing immediate-inclusion guarantees as the next spec-sheet battleground after TPS.
insights.quote: The goal is that if a valid transaction reaches the network on time, it should be included instantaneously.
insights.locator: This is why blockchain developers are moving

insights.claim: Strong Chain Quality, a concept and measure introduced by a16z crypto researchers, holds that a blockchain can reserve portions of each block for transactions surfaced through other parts of the network, giving valid transactions more than one route in and reducing single-operator control over who gets processed next.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A concrete, measurable spec to test protocol claims against — and a likely design requirement in institution-grade chains.
insights.quote: a blockchain can reserve portions of each block for transactions surfaced through other parts of the network
insights.locator: Our researchers introduced the concept and measure

insights.claim: Making blockspace behave like shared infrastructure with multiple routes in requires more complicated protocols than are run in production today, an explicit acknowledgement that the resilience fix is not yet shipped.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Timing risk: institutional-grade access guarantees remain research-stage, so near-term onchain venues still carry single-operator dependency.
insights.quote: This requires more complicated protocols than we run in production today, but the benefits may be worth it

themes.theme: Ordering discretion, MEV, and recreating TradFi asymmetries

insights.claim: In many of today's blockchain systems the block builder or proposer has substantial discretion over which transactions are included and in what order, a simplification that becomes unacceptable in markets where ordering determines priority, price, and execution fairness.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Proposer discretion is a concrete legal and best-execution obstacle for regulated institutions moving order flow onchain.
insights.quote: that party has quite a bit of discretion over which transactions are included and in what order
insights.locator: On many blockchains, transactions don’t become final one at a time

insights.claim: The institutional form of MEV is not exotic sandwich attacks but the simpler fact that whoever controls transaction flow can make decisions based on it before anyone else can.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Reframes MEV from a retail-DeFi nuisance into a market-structure governance issue institutions already know how to price.
insights.quote: The institutional version is simpler: whoever controls the flow can potentially make decisions based on it before anyone else can.
insights.locator: Moreover, if one party controls the next block

insights.claim: Without strong guarantees around ordering and execution rules, onchain markets risk recreating the exact flaws of existing market structure, where centralized intermediaries benefit from privileged access to order flow and trading intent.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: The bear case on tokenized markets is not technology failure but rent recreation — check who captures ordering rents in any onchain venue you back.
insights.quote: If onchain markets cannot provide strong guarantees around ordering and execution rules, they risk recreating the same asymmetries.
insights.locator: This starts to look a lot like the flaws

insights.claim: Protocol designers are pursuing explicit ordering rules of two kinds — deterministic rules based on priority fees, and application-specific rules set by the trading venue — aiming for precision comparable to the price-time priority of traditional venues.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Venue-set, application-specific ordering is a design pattern to look for in the next generation of onchain exchanges.
insights.quote: similar to price-time priority offered by traditional venues
insights.locator: Blockchain protocol designers are working on more explicit ordering rules

insights.claim: Inclusion and ordering guarantees are only valuable jointly: a fair sequencing rule fails if an auction bid or a liquidation can be selectively delayed before the rule is applied, and timely inclusion fails if participants cannot reason about treatment once in.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Diligence must test both guarantees together — a chain marketing one without the other offers no real execution assurance.
insights.quote: A fair sequencing rule isn’t helpful if an auction bid or a liquidation can be selectively delayed before the rule is ever applied.
insights.locator: Inclusion and ordering have to work together

insights.claim: The size and direction of an order reveals whether a fund is building or unwinding a position, so leaking it before full execution lets other traders move the price against that fund.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Information leakage is the binding constraint on large institutional flow going onchain — privacy tech is the unlock, not further speed.
insights.quote: The size and direction of an order, for instance, can show whether a fund is building or unwinding its position.
insights.locator: A participant’s trades can divulge what they know

insights.claim: Because many blockchains expose pending transactions before they are finalized, onchain finance specifically needs pre-execution privacy even where post-execution privacy is not technically achievable.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Public mempools are a structural disqualifier for institutional block trading; pre-execution confidentiality is the feature to underwrite.
insights.quote: many blockchains expose pending transactions before they’re finalized
insights.locator: This is especially relevant onchain

insights.claim: Timelock encryption and threshold encryption are the leading approaches for hiding transaction contents until a deadline passes or a committee confirms the transaction's block position is final, so the market only sees the trade when it is too late to front-run.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: A named, testable technology shortlist for screening privacy-layer and encrypted-mempool investments.
insights.quote: So by the time the market can see the transaction, it should already be too late to front-run it.
insights.locator: To that end, protocol designers are exploring

insights.claim: Disclosure rules can legitimately differ after execution — a public market might publish the full record while a bank makes a trade visible only to counterparties and regulators — provided parties who cannot see every detail can still verify the trade followed the rules.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Configurable post-trade disclosure is what lets regulated entities adopt shared ledgers; treat it as a product requirement, not a nice-to-have.
insights.quote: A public market might publish the full record, while a bank might make it visible only to the counterparties and regulators.
insights.locator: The goal for today’s protocol designers

insights.claim: Markets can be transparent without giving every participant a live preview of everyone else's unexecuted orders, so onchain finance should target auditability after execution combined with confidentiality before it.
insights.speaker: a16z crypto editorial
insights.so_what: Rejects the maximal-transparency default of most public chains — a design shift that favors chains offering selective disclosure.
